segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had finished saying all this in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A certain centurion had a slave whom he valued highly, and this slave was sick and about to die.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he heard about Jesus, he sent elders of the Jews to him, asking him to come and save his slave’s life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He is worthy to have you grant him this,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: for he loves our nation, and he himself built the synagogue for us.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Jesus went with them. He was already not far from the house when the centurion sent friends to say to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not fit to have you come under my roof.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: That is why I did not consider myself worthy to come to you either. But say the word, and let my servant be healed.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For I too am a man placed under authority, with soldiers under me. I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my slave, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus heard this, he was amazed at him. Turning to the crowd that was following him, he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the slave in good health.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a large crowd went along with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he approached the town gate, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow. A considerable crowd from the town was with her.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the Lord saw her, he was moved with compassion for her and said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not weep.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. He said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Young man, I say to you, rise!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “A great prophet has risen among us!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “God has come to help his people!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding region.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: John’s disciples reported all these things to him. And John, calling two of his disciples to him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: sent them to the Lord to ask,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the men came to him, they said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “John the Baptist has sent us to you to ask, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At that very time he healed many people of diseases, afflictions and evil spirits, and he granted sight to many who were blind.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go and report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, those with skin disease are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have good news proclaimed to them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And blessed is anyone who does not stumble because of me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When John’s messengers had left, he began to speak to the crowds about John:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What did you go out into the wilderness to look at? A reed shaken by the wind?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: What, then, did you go out to see? Someone dressed in soft clothing? Look, those who wear splendid clothes and live in luxury are in royal palaces.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: What, then, did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Look, I am sending my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way ahead of you.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I tell you, among those born of women there is no one greater than John; yet the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (All the people who heard, even the tax collectors, vindicated God, having been baptized with John’s baptism;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but the Pharisees and the experts in the law rejected God’s purpose for themselves, not having been baptized by him.)

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “To what, then, shall I compare the people of this generation? What are they like?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, who say, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a lament, and you did not weep.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Yet wisdom is vindicated by all her children.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee’s house and reclined at the table.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now there was a woman in the town who was a sinner. When she learned that he was reclining at the table in the Pharisee’s house, she brought an alabaster jar of perfume

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and stood behind him at his feet, weeping. She began to wet his feet with her tears, and she wiped them with the hair of her head, kissed his feet again and again, and anointed them with the perfume.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If this man were a prophet, he would know who and what kind of woman this is who is touching him, that she is a sinner.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Simon, I have something to say to you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Say it, Teacher.”

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Two people were in debt to a certain moneylender. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Since they could not repay, he canceled the debts of both. So which of them will love him more?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simon answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I suppose the one for whom he canceled the larger debt.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You have judged rightly.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then, turning toward the woman, he said to Simon,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do you see this woman? I came into your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not stopped kissing my feet.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with perfume.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For this reason, I tell you, her sins, many as they are, have been forgiven, for she loved much. But the one who is forgiven little loves little.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Your sins have been forgiven.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those reclining at the table with him began to say among themselves,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Who is this, who even forgives sins?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he said to the woman,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

notes.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by another, not a hired employee. ‘Servant’ became the usual English rendering when that word could cover both; today it suggests paid domestic work. Many modern translations and most scholars now use ‘slave’.
This is the same Greek word that in the plural is usually translated ‘Gentiles’. In the singular it means a people or nation, and here the Jewish elders use it of their own people.

The Greek form of address ranges from a polite ‘Sir’ to ‘Lord’ in the full religious sense. ‘Lord’ is the usual rendering here and fits the centurion’s marked deference, but the word alone does not show how much he meant by it.

The centurion’s message uses a different word here from the ‘slave’ of verses 2, 3, 8 and 10. It can mean ‘child’, ‘boy’ or ‘servant’. Since Luke identifies the person as the centurion’s slave, ‘servant’ is chosen. Some hear a note of affection in the word, though that is not certain.

The wording matches the Greek version of 1 Kings 17:23, where Elijah restores a widow’s son to life and gives him back to his mother. The crowd’s acclamation of ‘a great prophet’ in the next verse fits that echo.

In the Greek Scriptures this verb is used of God turning his attention to his people to rescue or care for them, a sense the modern English ‘visit’ no longer conveys. Most translations keep ‘visited’; a few render it along the lines chosen here.

The list echoes Isaiah’s descriptions of the time of God’s deliverance (Isaiah 35:5–6; 61:1; compare 26:19). Jesus answers John’s question not by claiming a title but by pointing to events that Scripture associated with that time.

The Greek term, following Leviticus 13–14, covers a range of skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean. It is not the same as modern leprosy (Hansen’s disease) and may not include it. That is why such people are said to be ‘cleansed’ and not simply healed. Most translations keep ‘lepers’, often with a footnote to this effect.

notes.phrase: does not stumble because of me
notes.traditional: is not offended in me / takes no offense at me
notes.note: The verb means to be tripped up or made to fall. Here it means being put off from trusting Jesus because he does not match expectations, which is stronger than the modern sense of taking offense. Several modern translations also use ‘stumble’.
The quotation combines Malachi 3:1 with wording from Exodus 23:20. The Greek word for ‘messenger’ is the one usually translated ‘angel’; it is also used of John’s own messengers in verse 24.

The verb belongs to a single Greek word-family that English splits between ‘righteous/just’ and ‘justify’. Here it means to acknowledge or show that God is in the right, and it recurs in verse 35 of wisdom. Other translations paraphrase, for example ‘acknowledged the justice of God’ or ‘declared God just’.

Verses 29–30 are taken here as Luke’s own aside, following the punctuation of the Greek edition and many modern translations. They can also be read as a continuation of Jesus’s speech. The Greek does not say what was heard: on the first reading it is probably Jesus’s words about John, on the second John’s preaching.
The term refers to specialists in the Law of Moses and its interpretation, not to courtroom advocates as ‘lawyers’ now suggests. Several modern translations render it as here.

notes.traditional: sat down to eat / took his place at the table
notes.note: At formal meals guests lay on couches, propped on one elbow, with their feet stretched out away from the table. This is how the woman can stand behind Jesus and yet be at his feet in verse 38.
A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s wage for a laborer (compare Matthew 20:2). The two debts are thus about five hundred and fifty days’ pay.

The Greek can be read as giving the cause of her forgiveness (she is forgiven because she loved) or the evidence for it (her love shows that she has been forgiven). The parable, in which love follows the canceling of the debt, and the second half of the verse favor the second reading, which most interpreters adopt. ‘For’ leaves both open, as the Greek does.

candidates.reason: Occurs throughout the New Testament, literally and as a metaphor for believers and apostles, and translations split between ‘servant’, ‘slave’ and ‘bondservant’.
Recurs across the Gospels and Paul with renderings varying among ‘offend’, ‘cause to stumble’ and ‘fall away’, and the noun σκάνδαλον needs to match.
‘Leper/leprosy’ misleads modern readers about the condition, and the choice must be uniform across the Synoptic healing stories.
God’s ‘visiting’ his people recurs in Luke–Acts (1:68, 1:78, 19:44; Acts 15:14) and elsewhere, and the traditional ‘visit’ no longer conveys the sense.
The vocative ranges from ‘Sir’ to ‘Lord’ when addressed to Jesus, and a consistent policy is needed for speakers who are not disciples.
